questions.question: What is the difference between gross profit and net income?
questions.questionHtml: What is the difference between gross profit and net income?

answers.text: Gross profit is revenue minus COGS; net income also subtracts operating expenses
answers.textHtml: Gross profit is revenue minus COGS; net income also subtracts operating expenses

answers.text: Net income is always higher than gross profit
answers.textHtml: Net income is always higher than gross profit

answers.text: Gross profit includes taxes; net income does not
answers.textHtml: Gross profit includes taxes; net income does not

questions.feedback: Gross profit = Revenue minus Cost of Goods Sold. Net income = Gross profit minus operating expenses (and other income/expenses). Net income is your true bottom line.
questions.feedbackHtml: Gross profit subtracts only COGS from revenue. Net income further subtracts all operating expenses.

questions.question: Why can a profitable business still fail?
questions.questionHtml: Why can a profitable business still fail?

answers.text: Because profits are taxed too heavily
Because it runs out of cash even though it is profitable on paper
answers.textHtml: Because it runs out of cash even though it is profitable on paper

answers.text: Because banks close accounts of profitable businesses
answers.textHtml: Because banks close accounts of profitable businesses

questions.feedback: A business can be profitable on paper but fail if clients pay late and cash is not available to cover ongoing expenses. Cash flow is king.
questions.feedbackHtml: Profitability on paper means nothing if you do not have cash available to pay bills. Cash flow is king.

answers.matchText: Whether cash is available to pay bills
answers.matchTextHtml: Whether cash is available to pay bills

answers.matchText: Snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity

questions.feedback: The P&L shows profitability, cash flow shows liquidity, and the balance sheet shows your financial position at a point in time.
questions.feedbackHtml: P&L = profitability. Cash flow = liquidity. Balance sheet = financial position snapshot.

questions.question: What is the safest approach to borrowing money from friends and family?
questions.questionHtml: What is the safest approach to borrowing money from friends and family?

answers.text: Always borrow from family first since they will not charge interest
answers.textHtml: Always borrow from family first since they will not charge interest

answers.text: Avoid it if possible; if you must, put everything in writing and ensure they understand the risk
answers.textHtml: Avoid it if possible; if you must, put everything in writing and ensure they understand the risk

answers.text: Borrow without formal terms to keep it friendly
answers.textHtml: Borrow without formal terms to keep it friendly

answers.text: Only borrow from family members you are not close with
answers.textHtml: Only borrow from family members you are not close with

questions.feedback: Most advisors recommend avoiding loans from friends and family entirely. If you must, formalize everything in writing and make sure they understand they may lose their investment.
questions.feedbackHtml: Avoid friends-and-family loans if possible. If necessary, formalize terms and communicate the risk clearly.

questions.question: Why is it better to overestimate expenses than to underestimate them?
questions.questionHtml: Why is it better to overestimate expenses than to underestimate them?

answers.text: It makes your business plan look more impressive to investors
answers.textHtml: It makes your business plan look more impressive to investors

answers.text: Because unexpected expenses are common and underestimating leads to cash shortfalls
answers.textHtml: Because unexpected expenses are common and underestimating leads to cash shortfalls

answers.text: Tax authorities prefer higher expense estimates
It helps you charge higher prices

questions.feedback: Small overlooked expenses add up quickly. Overestimating gives you a buffer against unexpected costs, while underestimating can create serious cash flow problems.
questions.feedbackHtml: Overestimating expenses creates a safety buffer. Underestimating leads to unpleasant surprises and potential cash shortfalls.
